title: Wanna Work Together?
speaker: Creative Commons narrator (not named)
intro: A short animated film about copyright and how Creative Commons licences let creators decide how other people may use their work.
summary: The film starts by showing how people such as teachers, artists and writers learn from and build on the work of others. It explains that when you create a photo, a song, a drawing, a film or a story, you get copyright automatically, so other people normally need your permission to use it, apart from cases of fair use. For creators who want their work to travel freely, full copyright can be too strict. Creative Commons offers free licences: on its website a creator answers a few questions, for example whether others may use the work commercially or change it, and gets a licence in about a minute. Creators keep their copyright, millions of works are now free to share and remix, and the film invites viewers to join this shared culture.

vocab.m: the legal right to control who copies, shares or sells a creative work
when someone officially says you may do something
an official document or statement that says what you are allowed to do
connected with business and making money
to take an existing work and change or combine it to make something new
limiting what people can do

syn.title: Summarise with synonyms

syn.model: The film explains that anyone who makes a photo, a song or a story owns the copyright automatically, so other people normally need permission to use it. For creators who want their work to travel widely, that can be too strict. Creative Commons assists them: they retain their copyright but set new terms. The process is fast, because on the website they answer a few questions, for example about commercial use and changes. The licence then informs the public what they are permitted to do. Today millions of works can be reused and remixed for free.

adv.title: Use three adverbs
adv.prompt: Summarise the video in 60–100 words. Use all three adverbs below.
adv.model: The film explains that creators automatically own the copyright to their photos, songs and stories, so other people usually need permission to use them. However, some creators want their work to be used freely. Creative Commons gives them free licences, and choosing one takes about a minute: they decide whether others may use the work commercially or change it. Ultimately, the aim is a richer shared culture where millions of works can be reused and remixed.

The narrator also stated that Creative Commons offered free licences and that a creator could choose one on its website in about a minute by deciding whether commercial use and changes were allowed. levels.intro: Anna gets an email about an important meeting. Is it good news or bad news? A story about work, rumours and job names.

levels.title: Try something new for 30 days
levels.speaker: Matt Cutts
levels.intro: A short, funny talk with a simple idea: pick something you have always wanted to do and try it for 30 days.
levels.summary: Matt Cutts felt stuck in a rut, so, inspired by Morgan Spurlock, he started trying something new for 30 days. He says 30 days is about the right time to add or remove a habit. He learned three things. First, time became more memorable: when he took a picture every day for a month, he remembered where he was each day. Second, his self-confidence grew as the challenges got harder: the desk-bound computer nerd started biking to work for fun and later climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa. Third, if you want something badly enough, you can do anything for 30 days: he wrote a 50,000-word novel in a month by writing 1,667 words a day. The book is awful, but now he can call himself a novelist. Finally, small, sustainable changes were more likely to stick than big, crazy ones; after 30 days without sugar he went straight back to it. He ends by asking: what are you waiting for? The next 30 days will pass anyway.

vocab.m: bored because you do the same things every day and nothing changes
something you do regularly, often without thinking
easy to remember because it is special
the feeling that you can do things well
possible to continue for a long time
(informal) try it

syn.title: Summarise with synonyms
syn.prompt: Write your own summary of the talk in 60–100 words. Replace every underlined word with a synonym.
syn.text: Matt Cutts [tried] something new for 30 days. His challenges made time more [memorable], and his self-confidence [grew]. He also [learned] that [small] changes [last] longer than big ones.
syn.model: Matt Cutts felt stuck in a rut, so he attempted something new for 30 days. When he took a photo every day, the month became unforgettable. Finally, he suggested that small changes were more likely to stick and asked what we were waiting for.

levels.title: Inside the mind of a master procrastinator
levels.speaker: Tim Urban
levels.intro: A very funny and surprisingly serious talk about why we leave things to the last minute, with three cartoon characters who live in your head.
levels.summary: Tim Urban, the writer behind the blog Wait But Why, describes himself as a master procrastinator: he had a year to write his 90-page senior thesis and wrote it in the last 72 hours, pulling two all-nighters. He explains the procrastinator's brain with three characters. The Rational Decision-Maker wants to do sensible things, but the Instant Gratification Monkey takes the wheel and only cares about what is easy and fun right now. They spend time in the Dark Playground, where leisure activities happen when they should not, so the fun is full of guilt, dread and anxiety. The only thing the Monkey fears is the Panic Monster, which wakes up when a deadline is close or there is a risk of public embarrassment. The bigger problem, Urban argues, is procrastination with no deadline, such as starting a career project, seeing family, looking after your health or working on a relationship: the Panic Monster never appears, so people quietly become spectators of their own lives. He shows a Life Calendar with one box for every week of a 90-year life and concludes that everyone is procrastinating on something, so we all need to stay aware of the Monkey, starting today.

vocab.m: to delay doing something you should do, often because it is unpleasant or difficult
the wish to have pleasure or a reward immediately, not later
to take control (literally: start driving)
a strong feeling of fear about something that is going to happen
not deserved, because you have not done the work for it
someone who watches something but does not take part

questions.why: He argues that we are all procrastinators and need to stay aware of the Instant Gratification Monkey, starting today.

listen.q: Explain the three characters in a procrastinator's brain.
listen.hint: Who wants to work, who wants fun, who is scary?
listen.model: There is a Rational Decision-Maker who wants to do sensible, productive things, an Instant Gratification Monkey who takes the wheel and only cares about what is easy and fun now, and a Panic Monster who wakes up near a deadline and frightens the Monkey away.

listen.q: Explain the Dark Playground.
listen.hint: What kind of fun happens there, and how does it feel?
listen.model: The Dark Playground is where leisure activities happen at times when they should not. Because the fun is unearned, it is full of guilt, dread, anxiety and even self-hatred.

listen.q: Explain the two kinds of procrastination and the Life Calendar.
listen.hint: With and without a deadline. What do the boxes show?
listen.model: With a deadline, the Panic Monster eventually appears and the work gets done. Without a deadline, for example with health or relationships, it never appears, so the procrastination can go on for ever. The Life Calendar has one box for each week of a 90-year life, which shows how limited our time is.

syn.title: Summarise with precise vocabulary
syn.prompt: Write a summary of the talk in 100–150 words. Replace every underlined word with a more precise or formal synonym.
syn.text: Urban [admits] that he [left] his thesis until the last minute. He [argues] that procrastinators are not [lazy], but that the [problem] becomes far more [serious] when there is no deadline.
syn.model: Tim Urban confesses that he put off his 90-page senior thesis until the final 72 hours. To explain why, he describes three characters in the procrastinator's mind: a Rational Decision-Maker, an Instant Gratification Monkey that takes control and chooses whatever is easy and pleasant, and a Panic Monster that only wakes up when a deadline approaches. In between, procrastinators spend their time in the Dark Playground, where leisure is unearned and therefore full of guilt and dread. Urban contends that procrastinators are not idle; they are caught in an internal struggle. However, the issue becomes far more alarming when there is no deadline at all, as with health, relationships or personal projects, because the Panic Monster never appears. His Life Calendar, with one box for every week of a 90-year life, is a reminder that time is limited.

rep.title: Formal report in reported speech
rep.prompt: Write a formal account of Urban's main points for a training newsletter at work (110–150 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: In his talk, Tim Urban acknowledged that he had written most of his senior thesis in the last three days before the deadline. He contended that procrastination was not a matter of laziness but of an internal conflict between a Rational Decision-Maker and an Instant Gratification Monkey, which preferred easy and enjoyable activities. He explained that the only thing the Monkey feared was the Panic Monster, which appeared when a deadline was approaching. He warned, however, that the most damaging form of procrastination occurred when there was no deadline at all, for example in relation to health, family or long-term ambitions. He concluded that everyone was procrastinating on something and recommended that people should remain aware of the Monkey, starting that very day.

arg.title: Argue a position
arg.prompt: 'Deadlines are the most effective cure for procrastination.' Write a formal argument (150–200 words). Use ideas from the talk, present the other side, and give your own view. No contractions.
arg.model: It is often argued that deadlines are the most effective cure for procrastination. Tim Urban's talk certainly supports this idea to some extent: the Panic Monster only wakes up when a deadline is close, and only then does the Instant Gratification Monkey let go of the wheel. Moreover, many students and employees would admit that a fixed date is what finally makes them start. However, this solution has clear limits. Work completed in a last-minute panic is rarely our best work, and the weeks before the deadline are spent in the Dark Playground, full of guilt and anxiety. Furthermore, as Urban points out, the most important things in life, such as health, relationships and personal projects, have no deadline at all. In my view, deadlines are therefore a useful tool rather than a cure. People who wish to stop procrastinating should create their own small, regular deadlines and, above all, remain aware of the Monkey before the Panic Monster is needed.

levels.title: Do schools kill creativity?
levels.speaker: Sir Ken Robinson
levels.intro: One of the most-watched TED talks ever: a witty, very British argument that education systems teach children out of their creativity.
levels.summary: Ken Robinson argues that creativity is now as important in education as literacy and should be treated with the same status. Children, he says, are not frightened of being wrong: a girl drawing a picture of God tells her teacher that people will know what God looks like in a minute. If you are not prepared to be wrong, you will never come up with anything original, yet schools and companies stigmatise mistakes, so, as Picasso suggested, we do not grow into creativity but are educated out of it. Every education system has the same hierarchy of subjects, with mathematics and languages at the top, then the humanities, and the arts at the bottom; even within the arts, art and music rank above drama and dance. He explains that public education was invented to meet the needs of industrialism and is designed to produce university professors, who, he jokes, live in their heads. Meanwhile academic inflation means degrees are worth less than before. He tells the story of Gillian Lynne, a girl who could not sit still at school: a specialist saw that she was a dancer, she went to dance school and became a choreographer behind Cats and The Phantom of the Opera. He concludes that we must see our creative capacities as a richness and educate the whole being of children so they can face the future.

vocab.m: the ability to read and write
to treat something as shameful or socially unacceptable

listen.hint: Children vs adults; what happens at school and at work?

By the time they become adults, most people have lost this capacity, because schools and companies stigmatise mistakes. listen.q: Explain the hierarchy of subjects and why it exists.
listen.hint: Which subjects are at the top and bottom? What historical reason does he give?

listen.q: Retell the story of Gillian Lynne and say what it shows.
listen.hint: School, the specialist, the result.
listen.model: Gillian Lynne could not concentrate or sit still at school, and her school thought she had a learning disorder. A specialist watched her move to music and told her mother that she was a dancer and should go to dance school. She became a famous choreographer, which shows that intelligence takes many forms.

syn.title: Summarise with sophisticated vocabulary
syn.prompt: Write a summary of the talk in 120–170 words. Replace every underlined word with a more sophisticated synonym.
syn.text: Robinson [claims] that schools [kill] creativity. He is [sure] that children are [born] with huge talent, but that education [teaches] them to be [afraid] of mistakes.
syn.model: Sir Ken Robinson contends that education systems stifle the creativity they ought to nurture. He is convinced that children are endowed with extraordinary talent and are not frightened of being wrong, as his anecdote about a girl drawing God illustrates. Yet, if one is not prepared to be wrong, one will never produce anything original, and schools, by stigmatising error, condition pupils to be fearful of mistakes. Echoing Picasso, he concludes that we do not grow into creativity but are educated out of it. He traces this to a hierarchy of subjects, with mathematics and languages at the summit and the arts, especially dance, at the bottom, a structure designed to meet the needs of industrialism. Academic inflation, he adds, has made degrees worth far less. The story of Gillian Lynne, who became a celebrated choreographer instead of being treated for a disorder, shows the cost of a narrow view of intelligence.

rep.title: Formal account in reported speech
rep.prompt: Write a formal account of the talk for an education journal (130–170 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: Sir Ken Robinson contended that creativity had become as important in education as literacy and that it should be accorded the same status. He observed that young children were not afraid of being wrong, and he illustrated this with the story of a girl who had insisted that people would soon know what God looked like. He argued that anyone who was not prepared to be wrong would never produce anything original, and he warned that schools and companies stigmatised mistakes. He asserted that every education system shared the same hierarchy of subjects, with the arts at the bottom, and he explained that this hierarchy had been designed to meet the needs of industrialism. He also remarked that academic inflation had reduced the value of degrees. Finally, he recounted the story of Gillian Lynne and concluded that education should develop the whole being of every child.

arg.title: Write a balanced argument
arg.prompt: 'Schools should give dance the same status as mathematics.' Write a formal, balanced argument (200–260 words). Engage with Robinson's ideas, present the strongest counter-argument, and reach a clear conclusion. No contractions.
arg.model: Sir Ken Robinson's claim that schools should teach dance every day, just as they teach mathematics, is deliberately provocative. It could be argued that it is also justified. Children learn through their bodies as well as their heads, and, as the story of Gillian Lynne shows, a pupil who cannot sit still may be gifted in ways a traditional curriculum never notices. Moreover, the hierarchy of subjects was designed for an industrial economy that no longer exists, so it is reasonable to question whether it still serves young people. Furthermore, collaboration, confidence and the willingness to make mistakes, which dance develops, are precisely the qualities employers now value. Admittedly, there are strong objections. Mathematics underpins science, technology and finance, and a pupil who leaves school without basic numeracy faces serious disadvantages in daily life. Timetables are also finite, so giving dance equal hours would inevitably reduce time for other subjects, and many schools lack trained teachers and suitable spaces. Nevertheless, these objections concern resources rather than principle. In my view, schools should not necessarily give dance identical hours, but they should give it equal respect: it should be assessed seriously, taught by specialists and never treated as a reward for finishing 'real' work. Ultimately, Robinson's argument is less about dance itself than about recognising that intelligence is diverse, and on that point he is convincing.
